Two Technologies. One Familiar Story.

The past few weeks have been a turning point in AI.

The New York Times drew a stark parallel between AI and nuclear weapons — pointing to the OpenAI agent swarm that broke containment and autonomously hacked Hugging Face. Then Anthropic's Dario Amodei published a remarkable call to pace the frontier — slow capability development, embed independent evaluators, and pursue coordinated global governance. Links in the comments.

I've been reading this through a different lens. Not nuclear. Agriculture.
Those of us who've worked in seeds have lived a version of this story. In the 1990s, GMO technology was concentrated in a handful of companies who genuinely believed — correctly, in many measurable ways — that they were solving hunger and reducing chemical inputs. But the technology moved faster than the public conversation. Science-based global governance lagged. And trust, once lost, proved extraordinarily hard to rebuild.

The parallels to AI are hard to ignore: a few companies controlling the frontier, founders who are genuine true believers, and public trust eroding in real time.

The lesson from biotech isn't that the technology was wrong. It's that the innovators didn't spend enough time helping the world understand the technology — and the industry paid a price in lost public trust and market access.

Amodei's call for AI governance is needed, but AI innovators also need to engage the public in conversation about the opportunities and threats of AI.

The window to shape public opinion on AI is open. It won't stay that way.

We have been building AI models for detecting agricultural biotic stresses for more than a decade. While large-scale labeled image datasets and high-performing models have become increasingly feasible for insects and weeds, curating massive labeled datasets for plant disease diagnosis remains a hard problem!

However, AI agents powered by frontier vision-language models offer a promising training-free and explainable alternative—provided they have access to a structured knowledge base of crop–disease-specific visual symptoms.

In our new work, we compiled one of the largest plant disease image datasets and complemented it with automatically generated, source-grounded symptom descriptions. 

Our SAGE dataset includes:
🌱 335 crops
 🦠 1,251 disease classes
 🖼️ ~839K images

We then show how this combination enables a training-free, explainable agentic reasoning system for diagnosing diseases across crops. Our agentic framework identifies anatomical context, narrows candidate diseases using crop-specific symptom knowledge, sequentially compares reference images, and produces an explainable reasoning trace.

Adding structured symptom knowledge improves diagnostic accuracy by 16.2 percentage points on average, with consistent gains across all evaluated crops.

Looking forward to seeing the community build Agentic AI tools using SAGE and push plant disease diagnosis toward more scalable and explainable solutions!

Scientific progress has always depended on decentralized knowledge assimilation — many researchers, labs, and communities generating local insights, sharing partial knowledge, and collectively advancing the frontier. With the rise of Agentic AI, this process will be dramatically accelerated.

In this work, we develop a theoretically grounded framework, ADKO, where multiple autonomous agents solve scientific optimization problems collaboratively. Each agent learns from local data and exchanges compact “knowledge tokens” instead of sharing raw data or full models. This enables privacy-preserving, communication-efficient, and sample-efficient collaboration across heterogeneous agents.

Looking forward to thoughts and feedback from the community!

I’m excited to share that our paper, “In-Context Adaptation of VLMs for Few-Shot Cell Detection in Optical Microscopy,” has been accepted in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (https://lnkd.in/gQkcXb7S). 

In this work, we study how recent vision-language models and multimodal large language models adapt to microscopy, a setting where cell types and imaging conditions often lie outside their pretraining distributions. We find that zero-shot performance remains limited under this domain shift, but in-context examples help meaningfully. One of our key findings is that these models perform better on unseen, out-of-distribution objects when a conventional detector first proposes candidate regions and the MLLM is used for region classification, rather than relying on fully end-to-end detection. We also introduce Micro-OD, a benchmark for few-shot cell detection in optical microscopy, which we hope will support further research on foundation models for biomedical imaging.

I’m grateful to have worked on this with an amazing team, and I want to thank Prof. Soumik Sarkar, Prof. Adarsh Krishnamurthy, Prof. Anwesha Sarkar , and all of my co-authors for their support, guidance, and collaboration throughout this work.

Excited to share our paper, "Driving as a screening aid: Scenario-based cognitive assessment in older drivers from driving video," got published in 𝘈𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘐𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘛𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.

Detecting dementia in older adults typically involves costly and time-consuming clinical visits. We introduce a scenario-based framework that uses pretrained vision models to extract behavioral features from everyday driving video and ranks roadway scenarios by how well they separate cognitively healthy from impaired drivers. Our findings suggest that cognitively demanding scenarios, such as freeway interchanges, are far more revealing than routine highway driving. This approach can turn a personal car into a passive, low-cost "screening aid" for continuous, non-invasive cognitive monitoring during everyday commutes.

I am immensely grateful to my co-authors: Guillermo Basulto, Jun Ha Chang, Shauna Hallmark, Matthew Rizzo, Anuj Sharma, Soumik Sarkar. Also, huge thanks to University of Nebraska Medical Center, Institute for Transportation at Iowa State University, National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Aging (NIA).

It has been a week since the incredible opportunity to attended the World Sustainable Energy Days 2026 in Wels. Since then, I have revisited the presentations from the conference share by the organizers. The reality is that amid conflicting interests, energy price shocks, and communities affected by geopolitical decisions, the energy transition has shifted from not just an environmental issue to an enginerring urgency, at least for the EU. WSED 2026 highlighted this urgent reality.

A key takeaway from the conference is that the strongest energy systems are those designed with a clear understanding of real-world challenges, embracing variable inputs, imperfect data, and human behavior. Overly complex systems without operational intelligence tend to be fragile and costly, and a successful energy community goes beyond solar panels and shared meters, it includes a data management system, financial model, governance structure, and local trust working together. Examining successful models in regions like Upper Austria raises questions about replicating these efforts in areas with low trust, particularly in communities facing energy insecurity. This highlights the vital connection between research and responsibility.

I stepped out of Stadthalle Wels carrying a clearer vision of what is possible and a commitment to share this understanding with neighbors, colleagues, community leaders, and policymakers who needed to have been in that hall too. The speed of the transition will not hinge on advancements in technology but on how deeply people grasp its personal significance today. 

It was great meeting up with my friend Rafael Rodrigues. Your work on ML-driven approaches for energy-efficient building classification and renovation continues to inspire me. Timilehin Ayanlade at Iowa State University will present, “WeedNet: A Foundation Model Based Global-to-Local AI Approach for Real-Time Weed Species Identification and Classification”

Early and accurate weed identification is critical for effective management, yet current AI-based approaches face challenges due to limited expert-verified datasets and the high variability in weed morphology across species and growth stages. We present WeedNet, a global-scale weed identification model designed to recognize a wide range of species, including noxious and invasive plants. WeedNet is an end-to-end real-time pipeline that integrates self-supervised pretraining, fine-tuning, and trustworthiness strategies to improve both accuracy and reliability. Building on this foundation, we introduce a Global-to-Local strategy: while the Global WeedNet model provides broad generalization, we fine-tune local variants such as Iowa WeedNet to target region-specific weed communities in the U.S. Midwest. 

Our evaluation addresses both intra-species diversity (different growth stages) and inter-species similarity (look-alike species), ensuring robust performance under real-world variability. We further validate WeedNet on images captured by drones and ground rovers, demonstrating its potential for deployment in robotic platforms. Beyond field applications, we integrate a conversational AI to enable practical decision-support tools for farmers, agronomists, researchers, and land managers worldwide. These advances position WeedNet as a foundational model for intelligent, scalable, and regionally adaptable weed management and ecological conservation.

A few weeks ago, Nikee Shrestha, a PhD student in my lab, got an unexpected email from the editors at Plants, People, Planet. The paper she co-led with Anirudha Powadi had been selected as the cover article for their July issue.

The photo shows Dr. Michael Tross (now at Corteva) in the middle of a Nebraska corn field setting up one of the giant ground control points we used to align UAV and satellite imagery. It's a striking image—and a reminder of the work it takes to connect in field agricultural research with the latest and greatest in artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Nikee and Anirudha analyzed data from over 20,000 maize plots grown across the US Corn Belt. At each site, drones were flown, yield was measured, and commercial satellite images taken within a few days of each flight were acquired and analyzed. The question was simple: could satellite data, which is getting cheaper, higher resolution, and more accessible every year, be used to detect genotype-level differences in crop performance?

In most cases, the answer was yes. Models built from satellite imagery matched the performance of those built from drone data, enabling yield predictions with fewer flights, less labor, and the potential to scale phenotyping to more remote or resource-limited sites.

This project was supported by USDA NIFA through both their High Intensity Phenotyping program and AIIRA - AI Institute For Resilient Agriculture.

You cannot validate on what you can't see.

An awesome new preprint from Iowa State University, covering the development of a foundation model for weed detection - WeedNet.

The group pre-trained a Vision Transformer (ViT) model on 14 million images from iNaturalist, achieving up to 91% accuracy across 1500+ weed species. With a global to local approach, the model achieved 97% when fine-tuned on a dataset of Iowa’s 85 common weeds.

Importantly though, the approach shows the value of open source data in ag. On entirely unseen data from WeedAI, with 15 overlapping species the model correctly predicted ~71% of labels.

So imagine replacing the 14M iNaturalist with a country-wide image dataset. Suddenly we’d have labeled photos of every weed at every growth stage, in every field and lighting condition from an entire region, allowing people to build a lot more with a lot less.

That is the value of open source data at very large scales. What if iNaturalist didn't exist?

With an expanded WeedAI, researchers could test models on local challenges instead of guessing at edge cases. Policymakers could see exactly where data gaps remain. Farmers would trust tools that were validated on their own regions. Startups and labs would build on a common benchmark instead of reinventing the wheel.

You need open data for validation and development - because you cannot validate on what you can't see.

A very interesting paper, and well worth reading.

Our paper, “Optimizing Navigation and Chemical Application in Precision Agriculture with Deep Reinforcement Learning and Conditional Action Tree”, has been published in Smart Agricultural Technology! 
https://lnkd.in/gGey-i8z


Summary:
We present Hierarchical Action Masking Proximal Policy Optimization (HAM‑PPO), a two‑tier reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize robotic pesticide management in precision agriculture. At the high level, HAM‑PPO directs the robot to prioritize which field regions to scout, efficiently identifying potential infestation zones. At the low level, it computes precise navigation and spraying actions to treat those areas. This hierarchically structured action space enables joint decision‑making for both movement and spraying under resource and observation constraints, letting the agent perform low‑cost exploration to refine noisy field priors before committing to treatment. We also incorporate conditional action masking, dynamically disabling infeasible moves to accelerate learning and enforce valid navigation.
Through a comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse biotic‑stress distributions and severity levels in row‑crop fields, we demonstrate that HAM‑PPO significantly reduces non‑target spraying, chemical usage, and operational costs compared to reactive and uniform‑spraying baselines.
HAM‑PPO further demonstrates robustness to noisy sensor data and adaptability to different field conditions, making it a versatile solution for real‑world deployment where observation uncertainty and variable infestation patterns are common.




Huge thanks to my advisor, Prof. Soumik Sarkar for his outstanding guidance and vision throughout this project. I’m also grateful to my co‑authors, Zhanhong Jiang, Joshua Waite, Sarah Jones, Hernán Torres Pacin, Arti Singh, Asheesh Singh, and Baskar Ganapathysubramanian, for their invaluable contributions to the research.

🚀 Excited to share our recent work on LCLA: Language-Conditioned Latent Alignment!

How can we leverage powerful vision-language models for robot control without retraining entire policies?

Our idea is simple:
First train a privileged expert policy using full state observations to learn a task-relevant latent representation for control. We then train a lightweight adapter on top of a frozen vision-language model to align image and language embeddings with this expert latent space.

At deployment, visual and language inputs are mapped through the VLM + adapter into the expert latent space, allowing us to reuse the frozen action head of the expert policy to produce robot actions.

This provides a structured way to connect multimodal foundation models with privileged control policies.

In this work, we study how recent vision-language models and multimodal large language models adapt to microscopy, a setting where cell types and imaging conditions often lie outside their pretraining distributions. One of our key findings is that these models perform better on unseen, out-of-distribution objects when a conventional detector first proposes candidate regions and the MLLM is used for region classification, rather than relying on fully end-to-end detection.
